chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ali ibn Ma'bad, from Dorost ibn Abi Mansour, from Fuzayl ibn Yasar who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'He Desires and Intends, and He does not Love and is not Pleased. He Desires that nothing come into being except through His Knowledge, and He Intends similarly; He does not Love that it be said He is the third of three, and He is not Pleased with disbelief for His servants.'

key_terms.أَرَادَ: Intended/Willed (irada) — divine intention or purposive will
key_terms.الْكُفْرَ: Disbelief (kufr) — rejection of God and His messengers
key_terms.ثَالِثُ ثَلَاثَةٍ: Third of three — reference to the Christian Trinitarian doctrine
key_terms.شَاءَ: Desired/Willed (mashi'a) — the broadest form of divine volition encompassing all existents
key_terms.يُحِبَّ: Love (mahabbah) — divine approval or approbation, distinguished from mere will

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about the difference between God's desire, will, love, and pleasure?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) draws a precise theological distinction between four divine attributes: Divine Desire (mashi'a/sha'a), Divine Will/Intention (irada/arada), Divine Love (mahabbah/yuhibb), and Divine Pleasure/Consent (rida/yardha). The Imam teaches that God's Desire and Will are universal — encompassing all that exists, since nothing comes into being except through His Knowledge and Will — yet His Love and Pleasure are conditional, as He neither loves shirk (polytheism, specifically the Christian claim that He is 'the third of three') nor approves of disbelief for His servants. This was a significant theological clarification relevant to the Shia community's engagement with Christian and Mu'tazilite theological debates of the era.
